claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at% Mo to CoCrFeNi will promote in situ formation of a MoO3-containing tribofilm during sliding.
The resulting tribofilm will be thin, adherent, and adaptive with temperature.
The Mo modification will significantly reduce coefficient of friction relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
The Mo modification will significantly reduce wear rate relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has a stable single FCC phase.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has good ductility.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi lacks an adaptive surface-film mechanism for high-temperature sliding.
At room temperature, the added Mo remains in solid solution.
Mo in solid solution preserves the alloy's mechanical properties at room temperature.
During thermally activated sliding in air, Mo can oxidize and MoO3 can occur in the surface oxide layer of CoCrFeNiMo.
MoO3 is a lubricious layered oxide that lowers interfacial shear.
The proposed MoO3-based film will limit both adhesive and abrasive wear.
Process optimization can keep the oxide layer thin and adherent and prevent excessive growth or spallation.
The adaptive MoO3-based tribofilm forms at high temperatures but remains minimal at lower temperatures.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi undergoes high-temperature sliding-performance degradation.
Cyclic shear and accumulated stress can fragment a protective oxide film, remove its protection, and increase material loss.
The proposed operating boundary is sliding in ambient air from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under a load of approximately 10 N.
Friction, wear, tribofilm thickness, adhesion, continuity, chemistry, and mechanical integrity can be measured to test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant friction and wear improvement, or failure to form a stable MoO3 tribofilm at high temperature, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes effective adaptive lubrication across the entire room-temperature-to-800 °C range to a MoO3-based tribofilm, while the structural mediator says that film forms at high temperature and remains minimal at lower temperature. The room-temperature mechanism only invokes solid-solution retention and does not explain the predicted low friction and wear there.
